content:
"In the sweltering heat of a Darwin night, the air thick with the scent of eucalyptus and the distant hum of cicadas, Dale Scott Walkinshaw stumbled through the shadows, his mind fogged by alcohol and adrenaline. The crash had happened so fast—one moment, he was laughing with the girl from the bar, the next, the world had spun violently, metal screeching against wood as the Toyota Hilux plowed into the palm tree. He could still hear the sickening thud of the impact, the way her body had jolted against his. Now, crouched behind the scrub, he cradled her limp form, her breath shallow, her skin clammy. He didn’t know her name. He didn’t even know if she’d live.

The flashing lights of the police cruiser cut through the darkness before he heard the sirens. Two officers stepped out, their boots crunching on the gravel as they surveyed the wreckage. Walkinshaw’s heart pounded. He knew the drill—handcuffs, the cold metal of the caged van, the suffocating heat of the backseat. He’d been there before. But this time, something was different. This time, he wasn’t alone in his panic.

The officers approached, their voices sharp with authority. ‘Step out from there, mate. Hands where we can see them.’ Walkinshaw hesitated, glancing down at the girl in his arms. Her eyelids fluttered, a weak groan escaping her lips. One of the officers radioed for an ambulance, but the other’s gaze locked onto Walkinshaw’s bloodshot eyes. ‘You’re drunk,’ he said, not a question. ‘Breath test. Now.’

The numbers on the breathalyzer glowed an accusatory red: 0.149. Walkinshaw barely registered the cuffs clicking around his wrists. All he could think about was the last time he’d been in a police van—the way the walls seemed to close in, the way the air had grown thin, the way he’d clawed at the door until his fingers bled. He’d survived that night. But he knew, deep down, that not everyone did.

As they loaded him into the back of the van, the girl’s faint whimpers still echoed in his ears. The door slammed shut, the lock engaging with a finality that made his stomach twist. The van lurched forward, the engine’s growl muffled by the thick metal walls. Walkinshaw pressed his forehead against the cage, his breath coming in ragged gasps. The heat was unbearable. The darkness, suffocating.

Somewhere in the back of his mind, he remembered the coroner’s words: *‘It wasn’t a matter of if a person would die in the back of a police van but when.’*

The van hit a bump, jostling him against the hard bench. His vision blurred. The girl’s face flashed before him—her pain, her fear. His own. The van rolled on, indifferent.

And then, silence."
